identification.summary: UNK_RemoteRogue is a Proofpoint temporary designation for a suspected Russian threat actor [S1][S4]. Proofpoint's April 2025 report on state-sponsored ClickFix use lists it alongside APT28 as the Russian examples, with Kimsuky (North Korea) and MuddyWater (Iran) [S2][S3]. Its ClickFix use is described as replacing existing installation and execution methods, not revolutionizing its operations; Proofpoint saw it use ClickFix once before reverting to traditional campaigns with similar targeting and infrastructure [S1][S3][S4]. It has a history of using compromised intermediate mail servers [S1][S4].
identification.firstObserved: December 2024 is the earliest dated activity found (ClickFix-themed campaign) [S2]. Earlier activity is implied by the 'traditional campaigns' language but is not dated in the sources gathered [S4].
identification.notes: The 'UNK_' prefix is Proofpoint's convention for an unclustered, unnamed actor; no Microsoft name or MITRE group ID was found. No aliases are stated by the cited sources. Proofpoint tracks it separately from APT28 [S2][S3]; do not merge the two.

attribution.confidence: Proofpoint (via press coverage) characterizes the actor as Russian or 'allegedly' Russian; this is a vendor assessment, not government attribution, and no state sponsor or agency is named in the sources gathered [S2][S3][S4].
attribution.basis: The basis for Proofpoint's Russia assessment is not stated in the secondary coverage and Proofpoint's original post could not be opened [S2][S3]. Observed Russian-language ClickFix instructions in the December 2024 lure are reported [S3].

sectors: Defense industrial base (two organizations closely related to a major arms manufacturer)
targeting.notes: In December 2024 the actor targeted two organizations closely related to a major arms manufacturer [S2][S3]. The manufacturer and the countries of the targets are not given in the secondary coverage reviewed. Proofpoint says its traditional campaigns share similar targeting, but does not enumerate it in the sources gathered [S1][S4].

capabilities.summary: In the December 2024 campaign, emails sent from compromised Zimbra servers and spoofing Microsoft Office carried a link to a fake Microsoft Word page with Russian-language instructions and a YouTube video tutorial [S2][S3]. Following the ClickFix instructions ran PowerShell that connected to a server running the Empire command-and-control framework [S2][S3]. The group has a history of using compromised intermediate mail servers, with an upstream concentrator at 80.66.66[.]197 noted [S1][S4]. Malpedia lists QuasarRAT against the actor [S4]; this could not be tied to a specific UNK_RemoteRogue intrusion (see gaps).

campaigns.name: ClickFix lure against arms-manufacturer-related organizations
campaigns.summary: Phishing from compromised Zimbra servers spoofing Microsoft Office led to a fake Word page with Russian-language ClickFix instructions; PowerShell then contacted an Empire C2 server. Two organizations closely related to a major arms manufacturer were targeted [S2][S3].

campaigns.name: Proofpoint report on state-sponsored ClickFix use
campaigns.summary: Proofpoint publishes 'Around the World in 90 Days' (dated 2025-04-17 per Malpedia's library entry), covering ClickFix use by Kimsuky, MuddyWater, APT28 and UNK_RemoteRogue between late 2024 and early 2025. It notes UNK_RemoteRogue reverted to traditional campaigns after one ClickFix use [S1][S2][S4].

diamond.adversary: Suspected Russian actor, unclustered and tracked by Proofpoint as UNK_RemoteRogue; sponsor unknown [S1][S4].
diamond.capability: Phishing with ClickFix social engineering, PowerShell execution, and the Empire C2 framework [S2][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised Zimbra mail servers as senders; compromised intermediate mailservers and an upstream concentrator at 80.66.66[.]197; a fake Microsoft Word landing page; an Empire C2 server [S1][S2][S3][S4].
diamond.victim: Two organizations closely related to a major arms manufacturer (December 2024) [S2][S3].
diamond.technology: Email infrastructure (Zimbra) used as a relay, Microsoft Office/Word branding as lure, and Windows PowerShell execution via user-pasted commands [S2][S3].

gaps: Proofpoint's original post could not be opened (host unreachable from the research environment); all report details come from press coverage and Malpedia [S2][S3][S4].
Date range of the covered ClickFix activity differs across secondary sources (late 2024 to early 2025 versus other windows); verify against the primary report.
Malpedia associates QuasarRAT with the report entry; the BleepingComputer summary ties QuasarRAT to Kimsuky, so its link to UNK_RemoteRogue is unverified [S3][S4].
Sponsor, Proofpoint's confidence level, and the evidence behind the Russia assessment are not public in the sources gathered.
Targeted country, specific arms manufacturer, objectives, and earlier non-ClickFix campaigns are not described in the sources gathered.
Relationship to APT28 or other Russian clusters and to vendor names (e.g. Microsoft) is unknown; none is stated in the sources.
Whether the Zimbra servers were compromised by this actor or by a third party is not stated.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain includes the email gateways and user endpoints of defense-industrial-base suppliers and subcontractors adjacent to major arms manufacturers [S2][S3]. STEP 2: The actor uses compromised third-party mail servers, so sender reputation is a weak filter [S1][S2]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is phishing from a compromised Zimbra server, Office-themed lure, user-run PowerShell (ClickFix), then Empire C2 [S2][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued low-volume targeted phishing of defense-related organizations, with ClickFix used opportunistically alongside traditional methods [S1][S4]. MDCOA (analyst judgment) is a shift to ClickFix at scale against DIB subcontractors. Candidate indicators: Office-spoofing links to fake Word pages with pasted-command instructions, PowerShell launched from the Run dialog or browser-initiated clipboard paste, outbound connections to Empire-style C2, and traffic to 80.66.66[.]197 [S1][S2][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track Proofpoint and DC3 reporting on ClickFix variants affecting DIB partners; the actor's targeting detail is thin, so treat as a watch item [S2][S4]. (2) Authorities: DIB contractor networks are largely outside DoD-owned DODIN, so reporting and defensive support run through DIB cybersecurity and DC3 channels. (3) Mission assurance: user training and endpoint controls limiting pasted PowerShell execution reduce exposure to this technique [S2][S3]. (4) Coordination: share the indicators with contractors and avoid merging this cluster with APT28 reporting [S2][S3].

provenance.importedSummary: UNK_RemoteRogue is a suspected Russian threat actor that has been observed utilizing ClickFix in its infection chains, although this technique is not revolutionizing their operations but rather replacing existing installation methods. The group has a history of employing compromised intermediate mailservers, with specific infrastructure noted, such as the upstream concentrator at 80.66.66[.]197. Proofpoint recorded their use of ClickFix only once before they reverted to traditional campaigns that share similar characteristics, including targeting and infrastructure. UNK_RemoteRogue has been linked to phishing activities and has shown consistent patterns in its operational tactics.
